text.p: - Over 65 percent of Slovenians think a new government line-up proposed by Prime Minister designate Janez Drnovsek will be approved by a parliamentary vote on February 27 or 28, a survey by daily Delo showed. Only 12.6 percent of those questioned did not think the proposal would be passed.

- Only the new ministerial candidates will have to go through fresh parliamentary hearings starting on Friday. Candidates from the previous government line-up that parliament rejected on February 6 will not be heard again.
- The government on Thursday refused a demand by company Geoplin to increase prices of natural gas by 16.5 percent.
- Interest is growing among successor states of the former Yugoslavia for international arbitration in dividing the assets of the federation, Miran Mejak, leader of Slovenia's negotiation group said.

- Slovenia's national radio and televison station (RTVS) said it would be able to cover its losses in the next five years. Its losses in 1996 rose to 1.4 billion tolars ($9.1 million) from 383 million tolars in 1995.
- Government spending on promoting tourism this year will reach 810 million tolars ($5.3 million), 3.65 times more than last year, the Center for the Promotion of Tourism said.
- The Slovenian church will have to pay 660 million tolars in administrative costs for the visit of Pope John Paul II to Slovenia last May.
- Janez Kocijancic, president of the opposition United List of Social Democrats, the former communist party, will not stand for a second term, the party's general secretary said.
- Slovenia's petrol trader Petrol recently registered its shares with the security registering office KDD and is expected to list its shares on the Ljubljana bourse soon.
- Advertising in Slovenian media rose by 52 percent in 1996 to 172.1 million marks, with more than half the total earned by television stations.
